title: Hotter US Inflation Forces the Fed's Hand Back onto the Table
summary:
September's US consumer price report showed inflation running at **3.7%**, a little above forecasts, with energy doing most of the damage but core prices also firmer than hoped.

It matters because the Fed had been signalling patience. The data undermines the idea that an energy shock can simply be looked through, and revives the argument that second-round effects are starting to build.
context:
- Petrol prices jumped sharply in the month and accounted for over half of the monthly rise. That links the inflation story directly to the Iran conflict and the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz.

- Core inflation, at **2.6%**, also edged above expectations, with both goods and services contributing. Economists worry this signals underlying price pressure that is becoming stickier, which is what central banks fear most.

- Officials had played down urgency for an October move before the release. The next policy meeting is on 27-28 October, and markets and some banks, including Citi, now see a further hike in December as the likelier path.

title: AI Credit Worries Spread from CoreWeave to Chipmakers Worldwide
summary:
Doubts about how the AI buildout is being financed moved to the centre of the tech debate this week. Shares in CoreWeave, which rents out AI computing capacity, fell sharply and its bonds weakened towards distressed levels.

The concern matters because much of the sector's spending is funded by debt, so any wobble in lenders' confidence can feed straight back into chip and data-centre demand.
context:
- AI infrastructure firms have borrowed heavily to buy chips and build data centres, betting that customers' demand will cover the interest bill. Higher bond yields make that bet more expensive, and this week's inflation data pushed rate expectations the wrong way.

- South Korea felt it most because the Kospi leans heavily on SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. The index had its worst week since 2008 after a huge run this year, and reports pointed to a Chinese memory-chip advance as an added worry.

- Chip stocks suffered a long losing streak and the Nasdaq had its worst week in months. Similar scares have faded before, but this one is about credit rather than valuation, which is harder to dismiss.

title: Hormuz Attacks Escalate as Emergency Stocks Struggle to Offset Supply Risk
summary:
Iran stepped up attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, while Houthi missiles and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries added further supply risk. Emergency stock releases from IEA members have been unable to restore confidence.

The story matters because it shows the oil market is now being driven by several overlapping disruptions at once, which is a more persistent problem than any single outage.
context:
- Tanker flows through Hormuz are reported to have recovered only to about **70%** of pre-war levels, according to Kpler. Attacks therefore threaten a fragile partial recovery rather than a normal market.

- IEA members agreed this week to finish releasing the remaining 100 million barrels from the intervention launched in March. Stock releases buy time but cannot replace a secure shipping route.

- Brent closed near **$110** on Friday, after trading around $106 earlier in the week. Energy is the main source of this year's inflation rebound, so oil now feeds directly into central bank decisions.
